Deimos. The smaller and more distant of Mars's two natural satellites, discovered in eighteen seventy-seven by Asaph Hall. Named after the Greek god of panic and dread, Deimos orbits Mars at a distance of approximately twenty-three thousand four hundred sixty kilometers—farther than the synchronous orbit radius—and moves so slowly that it takes nearly three Martian days to orbit the planet.

Deimos is about twelve kilometers in diameter, making it one of the smallest of Mars's moons. It has a very low density and porous composition, and is likely a captured C-type asteroid that was drawn into Mars's gravity well long ago. The surface is smoother and less cratered than its sibling moon Phobos, and it is covered in regolith, a thick layer of dust that blankets the terrain.

Because Deimos orbits slower than Mars rotates, from the Martian surface Deimos appears nearly stationary in the sky. Retrograde orbital studies suggest it may have been captured from the asteroid belt rather than forming with Mars in the early solar system. Asaph Hall discovered Deimos in eighteen seventy-seven, nine days after his discovery of Phobos. The name comes from the Greek word for dread, and along with Phobos represents the two aspects of fear in ancient mythology.
